title: FRM Quant, Lesson 1: Stationarity and AR, MA models - the precondition for any forecast
subtitle: Regressing two non-stationary series gives a beautiful R² and a meaningless conclusion
whyItMatters: Every time series model in FRM - from GARCH to interest rate forecasting - rests on an assumption of stationarity. Skipping that check is the source of spurious regression, the kind of result that looks most convincing and is entirely wrong.
openingQuestion: Regressing the price of stock A on the price of stock B gives an R² of 0.92 even though the two companies have nothing to do with each other. What is the most likely cause?
openingOptions: The two companies really do share an economic link nobody has found
Spurious regression, because both price series are non-stationary
The sample is too small, so the coefficient is badly estimated
The standard errors were miscalculated, which inflated the R²
explanation: Two series that both trend upward through time will always correlate strongly even with no causal relationship at all - this is spurious regression. The high R² here reflects the fact that both drift with time, not any link between them. The remedy is to test for stationarity first, and if a series is non-stationary take the first difference, which turns prices into returns, before running the regression.

diagram.label: Test for stationarity before doing anything else
If non-stationary, take differences - prices become returns
Identify the model orders using the ACF and the PACF
Check whether the residuals still carry autocorrelation

realWorldExample.company: Forecasting interest rates with a time series model
realWorldExample.description: The level of interest rates is usually non-stationary while the change in rates is stationary. A model built on levels produces a forecast that drifts without limit through time; a model built on changes produces one that reverts to a mean. Same data, two completely different conclusions, and the only difference is the stationarity check.

quiz.question: What conditions must a weakly stationary series satisfy?
options: A mean and a variance that stay constant through time
A mean of exactly 0 and a variance of exactly 1 at every point
Complete independence between every value in the series
A normal distribution holding at every point in the series
quiz.explanation: Weak stationarity requires only that the first two moments stay stable through time and that the covariance between two points depends solely on the distance between them. It demands no normal distribution and no independence - autocorrelation is entirely permitted, provided its structure does not change over time. Fixing the mean at zero and the variance at one describes a standardised series, which is a different requirement altogether.

quiz.question: What is the core difference between an AR(1) model and an MA(1) model?
options: AR suits stationary series while MA suits non-stationary series
AR regresses on past values, MA regresses on past shocks
AR always needs more parameters than an MA of the same order
AR applies to returns while MA applies to volatility
quiz.explanation: AR says today's value depends on yesterday's value; MA says it depends on yesterday's random error. The practical consequence: a shock in an AR model decays geometrically and lingers indefinitely, while in an MA(q) it disappears completely after q periods. Both forms require stationarity, an AR(1) and an MA(1) each carry one parameter, and neither is tied to a particular quantity such as returns or volatility.

quiz.question: What is the stationarity condition for an AR(1) model with coefficient φ?
options: φ must exceed 1 for the series to revert to its mean
φ must be a positive number between 0 and 1
The absolute value of φ must be smaller than 1
φ must equal 0 for the series to have no trend at all
quiz.explanation: With |φ| < 1, the effect of a shock is multiplied by φ each period, so it decays and the series returns to its mean. At exactly 1 it becomes a random walk - the shock never decays and the series is not stationary. Above 1 the series diverges. A negative φ is still stationary; the series simply oscillates back and forth around the mean rather than approaching it from one side.

quiz.question: What are the ACF and the PACF used for in the model identification process?
options: Comparing forecast quality between two competing specifications
Checking whether the series follows a normal distribution
Computing robust standard errors for the regression coefficients
Guessing the orders p and q before the estimation step
quiz.explanation: An ACF that decays with a PACF that cuts off after lag p signals an AR(p); conversely an ACF cutting off after q with a decaying PACF signals an MA(q). This is the identification step, not the conclusion - you still have to estimate the model and then inspect the residuals. Forecast comparison happens after estimation, distributional shape is a separate diagnostic, and robust standard errors belong to a different problem entirely.

quiz.question: After estimating a time series model, what is the most important check on the residuals?
options: That the residuals carry no statistically significant autocorrelation left
That the residuals have a mean of exactly zero on the sample
That the residuals have a larger variance than the original series
That the residuals correlate strongly with the dependent variable
quiz.explanation: If the residuals still show autocorrelation, the model has not extracted all the forecastable structure in the data - information has been left behind. This is why the Ljung-Box test on residuals is a required step rather than an optional one. A zero mean follows mechanically from including an intercept, residual variance smaller than the original is the whole point of fitting, and residuals correlating with the dependent variable would be a symptom of the same failure.

practicePrompt.question: Regressing a house price index on the number of films screened each year, over 2010-2024, gives an R-squared of 0.89 and a very large t-statistic. What is the correct conclusion?
options: Both series trend upward, so this is a spurious regression result
There is a real economic link; find the transmission channel
An R-squared of 0.89 is not high enough to conclude anything
Add control variables and the coefficient will become sensible
practicePrompt.explanation: Two non-stationary series that both rise through time will produce a high R-squared and a very large t-statistic even with no relationship between them - the only thing the regression has found in common is time itself. That is spurious regression, and the dangerous part is that it leaves no trace on any of the familiar numbers: a lovely R-squared, a lovely t, everything looking like a discovery. Testing for stationarity is therefore the FIRST step rather than a final diagnostic - skip it and every number afterwards is computed correctly on the wrong question. The usual remedies are differencing or a cointegration test.

keyTakeaways: Two series that both trend will correlate strongly even when unrelated - that is spurious regression
Weak stationarity: stable mean and variance, with covariance depending only on the lag
AR regresses on past values and its shocks decay; MA regresses on shocks and they vanish after q periods
The stationarity condition for AR(1) is |φ| < 1; at exactly 1 it is a random walk and non-stationary

summary.keyIdea: Testing for stationarity is the first step, not a final diagnostic. Skip it and every number afterwards is computed correctly on the wrong question.

application.message: When you see a forecasting model built on price levels or rate levels rather than on their changes, be suspicious before you read the results. It is a sign the stationarity check was skipped.

sections.text: Regress any two price series against each other over a long enough window and you will very likely get a beautiful R². That says nothing about the two companies - it says both of them went up over time.
Why a trend fools a regression

A regression looks for a relationship between two variables, but if both drift in the same direction it picks up that drift and calls it a relationship. This is not a sample size problem and more data will not fix it - more data simply makes the coefficient look even more significant.

The most common remedy is to take the first difference. For prices, the first difference is the return - and that is why almost every financial model works on returns rather than on prices. This step is not a convention adopted for convenience, it is the condition that makes the regression meaningful.
AR and MA: two ways a series remembers its past

AR says today depends on yesterday, so a shock decays geometrically and in theory lasts forever. MA says today depends on yesterday's surprise, so a shock vanishes completely after q periods. Choosing the wrong form means describing the wrong memory - and long-horizon forecasts will be wrong in a systematic direction.

sections.label: Worth remembering
sections.text: Rate levels are usually non-stationary, rate changes are stationary. A model built on levels forecasts an unbounded drift; one built on changes forecasts a return to the mean. Same data, two different worlds.
